## Identifying STS in AIS data
<!-- src: Week 3 - Spatial Data.pptx slide 11 -->

::: {.columns}
:::: {.column width="29%"}
- A simple algorithm:
- **If** two or more ships
- **Spend** two or more hours
- **Within** 500m of each other
- **Then** link them together
::::
:::: {.column width="71%"}
![](img/w03/w03_88d6515afa.gif){.pic style="max-height:700px"}
::::
:::

## Satellite detections + AIS
<!-- src: Week 3 - Spatial Data.pptx slide 14 -->

::: {.columns}
:::: {.column width="58%"}
- 33,273 satellite detections since 2021
- Cross-referencing the satellite detections with AIS data shows close agreement.
    - Satellite image metadata used to filter AIS data ± 24h of the time when the image was taken, within 500m of the center of the detection.
    - Draught data from AIS used to infer direction of cargo transfer
- However, instances of *disagreement* between AIS + RS data are interesting…

# Raster Data
<!-- src: Week 3 - Spatial Data.pptx slide 27 -->

## Raster Data: Definition
<!-- src: Week 3 - Spatial Data.pptx slide 28 -->

- Similar to a digital photograph. The entire area of the map is subdivided into a grid of tiny cells, or pixels. A value is stored in each of these cells to represent the nature of whatever is present at the corresponding location on the ground.
- The major use of raster data involves storing map information as digital images, in which the cell values relate to the pixel colors of the image. To reproduce the image the computer reads each of these cell values one by one and applies them to the pixels on the screen.

# Analytical Approaches
<!-- src: Week 3 - Spatial Data.pptx slide 45 -->

## Arithmetic {.smaller}
<!-- src: Week 3 - Spatial Data.pptx slide 48 -->

- Zonal Statistics
    - Vector-Vector
        - Calculate the number of vectors within another vector
            - e.g. count the number of tube stations (points) within each borough (polygon)
        - We can add attribute information;
            - E.g. calculate the average vote share in a 10km grid cell
    - Vector-Raster
        - Calculate the value of a raster within each polygon
            - e.g.  Calculate the average pixel value of nighttime lights within each 10km grid cell
- Raster math
    - Add/subtract/divide/multiply one raster by another
        - E.g. subtract nighttime lights imagery taken in 1992 from imagery taken in 2012 to see which areas have become more luminous
- Algorithms

## Broad Street Pump

::: {.columns}
:::: {.column width="42%"}
- During the **1854** cholera outbreak in London, Dr John Snow noticed a pattern in the spatial distribution of cases
- Infections were concentrated around a single water pump on Broad Street, in Soho

## Raster Math
<!-- src: Week 3 - Spatial Data.pptx slide 52 -->

- E.g. Nighttime Lights data
- Satellite images of the earth at night
    - Highly correlated with development indicators
- Applications:
    - Assessing economic development
    - Gauging the extent of destruction during war
    - Identifying refugee camps
    - Tracking methane flaring from oil production
- [Demo](https://worldview.earthdata.nasa.gov/?v=33.66968063480002,35.29300939693471,42.39486992011477,39.832834446950045&t=2012-01-01-T00%3A00%3A00Z&t1=2016-12-11-T00%3A00%3A00Z&l=VIIRS_Black_Marble,VIIRS_SNPP_CorrectedReflectance_TrueColor,MODIS_Aqua_CorrectedReflectance_TrueColor(hidden),MODIS_Terra_CorrectedReflectance_TrueColor(hidden)&l1=Reference_Labels(hidden),Reference_Features(hidden),Coastlines,VIIRS_Black_Marble,VIIRS_SNPP_CorrectedReflectance_TrueColor(hidden),MODIS_Aqua_CorrectedReflectance_TrueColor(hidden),MODIS_Terra_CorrectedReflectance_TrueColor(hidden)&ca=true&cm=spy)

## {background-image="img/w03/w03_d302cc7fccc00e9.png" background-size="contain"}
<!-- src: Week 3 - Spatial Data.pptx slide 53 -->

## Regression
<!-- src: Week 3 - Spatial Data.pptx slide 57 -->

- You can use spatial data to generate your own data for use in a regression
- Using zonal statistics, you can generate a table in which each row is an areal unit (e.g. province, grid-cell, etc.)
- But, beware of **AUTOCORRELATION**
    - **Things that are closer together (both in space and time) have more in common than things that are farther away.**
    - Statistical approaches generally assume that observations are *independent.*

# What Is a Network?
<!-- src: Week X - Networks.pptx slide 8 -->

## {background-image="img/w03/networks_slide_009.jpg" background-size="contain" .fallback}
<!-- src: Week X - Networks.pptx slide 9 -->


::: notes
Slide text: Networks Are Everywhere · Transport · Stations linked by track · Shipping · Vessels linked by cargo transfers · Friendship · People linked on Facebook, mapped by county · Neighbourhoods · Cross-class friendships in London · Every network is a set of nodes (things) and edges (relationships between them)
:::

## The Vocabulary
<!-- src: Week X - Networks.pptx slide 10 -->

![](img/w03/networks_66b680b4ca.png){.r-stretch fig-align="center"}

- **Node** (or vertex): a thing.   **Edge** (or link): a relationship.   **Degree**: how many edges a node has.
- **Directed**: A → B isn't B → A.   **Weighted**: edges have a strength or cost.

## Networks as Data
<!-- src: Week X - Networks.pptx slide 11 -->

::: {.columns}
:::: {.column width="66%"}
![](img/w03/networks_fe9fcc505b.png){.pic style="max-height:453px"}

- **Adjacency matrix**: a 1 where two nodes are connected. Good for maths, wasteful for big sparse networks.
- **Edge list**: one row per edge. This is what you'll usually load with pandas.
::::
:::: {.column width="34%"}

| source | target | min |
|---|---|---|
| Gt Portland St | Euston Sq | 2 |
| King's Cross | Euston Sq | 2 |
| King's Cross | Euston | 2 |
| Warren St | Euston | 1 |
::::
:::

## A Few Hubs, Many Ordinary Nodes
<!-- src: Week X - Networks.pptx slide 12 -->

![](img/w03/networks_032df417f1.png){.r-stretch fig-align="center"}

The London Underground is **regular**: every station has 1–7 neighbours. Kerch is **heavy-tailed**: the median vessel has 6 transfer partners, the top 1% over 67, the busiest 115. Big bulk carriers act as **hubs** that many small ships load into

## It's a Small World {.smaller}
<!-- src: Week X - Networks.pptx slide 13 -->

::: {.columns}
:::: {.column width="60%"}
![](img/w03/networks_39d955e93a.png){.pic style="max-height:484px"}

|  | Kerch | Random network |
|---|---|---|
| Average path length | 3.3 | 2.95 |
| Clustering coefficient | 0.324 | 0.015 |
::::
:::: {.column width="40%"}
- Compare with a **random network** with the same number of nodes and edges.
- Paths are about as short, but **clustering** is ~20× higher: a ship's partners also trade with each other.
- Short paths + high clustering = a **small world**. Milgram (1967): 'six degrees of separation'. Facebook (2016): 3.6.
::::
:::

::: notes
Largest connected component of the Kerch network vs one Erdos-Renyi G(n,m) draw (seed 1). Milgram (1967) Psychology Today; Bhagat et al. (2016) Facebook Research, 3.57.
:::

# Who Matters? Centrality
<!-- src: Week X - Networks.pptx slide 14 -->

## {background-image="img/w03/networks_slide_015.jpg" background-size="contain" .fallback}
<!-- src: Week X - Networks.pptx slide 15 -->


::: notes
Slide text: Three Ways to Be Central · Degree · How many connections? The popular one. · Betweenness · Share of shortest paths that pass through you. The broker. · Eigenvector · Connected to other central nodes. The insider. (Google's PageRank is a version.)
:::

## Which Ships Are Central?
<!-- src: Week X - Networks.pptx slide 16 -->

::: {.columns}
:::: {.column width="43%"}
- Top 25 by **degree**: half bulk carriers, half general cargo. The busy loaders
- Top 25 by **betweenness**: **40% tankers**, vs 24% of all ships. Tankers are the **brokers** linking otherwise separate groups
- Top 25 by **eigenvector**: 72% small general-cargo ships in the dense core
- Different measures pick out different **roles**
::::
:::: {.column width="57%"}
![](img/w03/networks_3e2e16bda8.png){.pic style="max-height:700px"}
::::
:::

::: notes
Top 5 by betweenness: Vladimir Monomakh, Kavkaz II, Horasan, Barla, Avior. Top 5 by degree: Venera, Barla, Horasan, Vladimir Monomakh, Kavkaz II.
:::

## The Broker in the Dark
<!-- src: Week X - Networks.pptx slide 17 -->

::: {.columns}
:::: {.column width="57%"}
- The **highest-betweenness** vessel is a Russian crude tanker, the \*Vladimir Monomakh\*
- Here it sits alongside another tanker that **isn't broadcasting AIS**
- Its draught drops (bottom): it has **unloaded**. The partner is invisible in the network
- The network only contains what AIS can see
::::
:::: {.column width="43%"}
![](img/w03/networks_bd3d58031a.png){.pic style="max-height:700px"}
::::
:::

## Does Centrality Flag Grain Ships?
<!-- src: Week X - Networks.pptx slide 18 -->

::: {.columns}
:::: {.column width="43%"}
- The 15 vessels named in media reports: median at the **90th percentile** by degree, 91th by eigenvector
- **7 of 15** are in the top 10% by degree
- Sanctioned vessels (purple) are mostly **below** the median: they transfer less, or less visibly
- Centrality can **prioritise** investigation. It can't prove anything
::::
:::: {.column width="57%"}
![](img/w03/networks_42ca993af0.png){.pic style="max-height:700px"}
::::
:::

# Finding Communities
<!-- src: Week X - Networks.pptx slide 30 -->

## Communities: Clustering for Networks
<!-- src: Week X - Networks.pptx slide 31 -->

::: {.columns}
:::: {.column width="43%"}
- A **community**: many edges **inside**, few **between**
- Groups nodes by their **connections**, not their features (feature-based clustering comes in Week 10)
- **Modularity**: how much denser than chance (above ~0.3 is notable)
- **Louvain** (2008): merge whatever raises modularity most
- London Underground: **9** communities (Q = 0.76). No coordinates used, yet they're **geographic**
::::
:::: {.column width="57%"}
![](img/w03/networks_5783449bcf.png){.pic style="max-height:700px"}
::::
:::

## Communities Are Cargo Markets
<!-- src: Week X - Networks.pptx slide 33 -->

::: {.columns}
:::: {.column width="47%"}
![](img/w03/networks_a94182f0d3.png){.pic style="max-height:634px"}

Colour = community; red rings = vessels named in grain reports
::::
:::: {.column width="53%"}
![](img/w03/networks_ee18f3dff9.png){.pic style="max-height:451px"}

- 721 vessels, 4,008 transfer pairs (2022-02 to 2023-08). Louvain: 7 communities, modularity 0.59.
- The algorithm never saw vessel type, yet two communities are **almost all tankers** (97%, 87%)
::::
:::

::: notes
Communities are the stored Louvain labels from the Bokeh page (modularity recomputed here on the largest component). Dry-cargo communities mix small general-cargo/river-sea ships with larger bulk carriers.
:::
